fields.heading: Who we help in Calgary
fields.body: We treat runners, cyclists, skiers, gym goers, youth athletes, and weekend warriors across northeast Calgary and the wider city. Common issues include sprains, strains, tendonitis, overuse injuries, and post surgical sports rehab.

fields.heading: Our approach
fields.body: Your recovery starts with a thorough movement and strength assessment. We identify the root cause, not just the painful area, then build a staged plan covering pain relief, mobility, strength, and sport specific return to play progressions.

fields.heading: Physiotherapy and massage treatments
fields.body: Depending on your injury, your plan may include manual therapy, dry needling, exercise prescription, massage therapy, and chiropractic care. All services are available at our Calgary physiotherapy and massage clinic in Calgary.

fields.heading: WCB and workplace injuries
fields.body: Workers Compensation Board Alberta covers many workplace injuries. If your claim is accepted, physiotherapy and massage therapy can play a central role in your recovery plan. Bring your WCB claim number and any paperwork to your first visit.

fields.heading: Common work injuries we treat
fields.body: Back and neck strain from lifting or desk work, repetitive strain injuries, falls, shoulder injuries, and post incident deconditioning are common in Calgary workplaces, from construction and trades to office and healthcare settings.

fields.heading: Return to work focus
fields.body: We align treatment with your job demands, whether that means sitting tolerance, lifting capacity, standing endurance, or driving. Progress is documented so you, your employer, and WCB have a clear picture of your recovery.

fields.heading: Pre surgery and after surgery care
fields.body: Strengthening before surgery can improve outcomes. After your procedure, we follow surgeon protocols while adapting to your progress, managing swelling, scar tissue, range of motion, and gradual loading.

fields.heading: Surgeries we commonly rehab
fields.body: ACL and meniscus repair, rotator cuff surgery, hip and knee replacement, spinal surgery, fracture fixation, and arthroscopic procedures are familiar territory for our Calgary team.

fields.heading: Your recovery timeline
fields.body: Rehab is phased: early protection and range of motion, then strength and control, then return to daily activities, work, and recreation. We set realistic milestones and adjust your program every visit.

fields.heading: Conditions we address
fields.body: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, vestibular neuritis, balance loss after injury or illness, age related balance decline, and dizziness linked to neck or concussion issues.

fields.heading: Vestibular rehabilitation
fields.body: Vestibular physiotherapy uses specific head movements, habituation exercises, and balance training to retrain your brain and inner ear system. BPPV can often improve significantly within one to three sessions.

fields.heading: Fall prevention in Calgary
fields.body: For older adults and anyone at fall risk, we assess gait, strength, and reaction time, then build a practical program to improve stability at home and in the community.

fields.heading: During pregnancy
fields.body: Low back pain, SI joint pain, rib discomfort, carpal tunnel symptoms, and pelvic girdle pain are common. We use safe manual techniques, taping, exercise, and education to keep you comfortable and active through all trimesters.

fields.heading: After birth
fields.body: Postnatal care covers pelvic floor recovery, abdominal separation, cesarean or perineal scar management, breastfeeding posture, and gradual return to walking, running, or gym training when you are ready.

fields.heading: Pelvic health connection
fields.body: Many pregnancy and postnatal issues overlap with pelvic floor function. Our team coordinates pelvic health assessment with your broader physiotherapy and massage plan.

fields.heading: A whole person approach
fields.body: Chronic pain is influenced by tissue health, nervous system sensitivity, stress, sleep, and activity levels. We address all of these with a plan that goes beyond short term relief.

fields.heading: Conditions we support
fields.body: Persistent back and neck pain, fibromyalgia, headaches, arthritis discomfort, neuropathic pain, and pain after injury that has not fully resolved.

fields.heading: Building capacity over time
fields.body: Graded exercise, pacing strategies, massage therapy, manual therapy, and pain education help you do more of what matters, whether that is working, hiking in the foothills, or playing with your kids.

fields.heading: Who benefits from pelvic physiotherapy
fields.body: Women and men of all ages, including postpartum patients, perimenopausal women, athletes with pelvic floor dysfunction, and men after prostate surgery.

fields.heading: What to expect
fields.body: Your first visit includes a detailed history and, with your consent, an internal or external assessment of pelvic floor muscle function. Treatment may include exercise, manual techniques, breathing coordination, and lifestyle modifications.

fields.heading: Common goals
fields.body: Reduce leakage with cough, sneeze, or sport; lessen pelvic pain; improve core and floor coordination; prepare for or recover from childbirth; return to intimacy without discomfort.

fields.heading: Symptoms we help manage
fields.body: Headache, dizziness, brain fog, light and noise sensitivity, neck pain, balance issues, and exercise intolerance after concussion.

fields.heading: Graduated return to activity
fields.body: Rest is important early on, but prolonged inactivity can delay recovery. We guide a structured progression back to cognitive and physical activity based on your symptoms.

fields.heading: Vestibular and neck care
fields.body: Many post concussion symptoms involve the neck and balance systems. Our team integrates vestibular rehab and cervical treatment when indicated.

fields.heading: How acupuncture helps
fields.body: Fine needles stimulate specific points to modulate pain signals, reduce muscle tension, support circulation, and promote relaxation. Modern research supports its use for many musculoskeletal and stress related conditions.

fields.heading: What we treat
fields.body: Back and neck pain, headaches, arthritis discomfort, sports injuries, stress and insomnia, and complementary support alongside physiotherapy or massage therapy.

fields.heading: Your first session
fields.body: We review your health history, discuss goals, and explain the treatment process. Most patients find acupuncture comfortable and leave feeling relaxed.

fields.heading: MVA injuries we treat
fields.body: Whiplash and neck pain, headaches, mid back and low back pain, shoulder and rib injuries, jaw tension, dizziness, and soft tissue strains are common after rear end collisions, T bone impacts, and multi vehicle accidents on Calgary roads. Symptoms may appear immediately or develop over the days following a crash.

fields.heading: Alberta insurance and your claim
fields.body: Alberta has a regulated automobile insurance system for accident benefits. If you were injured in a collision, you may be eligible for coverage for approved treatment such as physiotherapy and massage therapy through your automobile insurance claim. Bring your claim details, policy information, and any forms from your insurer or adjuster to your first visit.

fields.heading: Your assessment and treatment plan
fields.body: We start with a thorough history of the accident, your symptoms, and how they affect sleep, work, and driving. Your assessment covers movement, strength, posture, and any red flags that need medical follow up. Treatment may include manual therapy, exercise rehab, massage therapy, acupuncture, and education on pacing and home recovery.

fields.heading: Whiplash and early treatment
fields.body: Early, appropriate care after whiplash often leads to better outcomes than prolonged rest alone. We guide you through gradual mobility, strengthening, and return to activity while monitoring symptoms such as headaches, arm pain, or dizziness that may need coordinated care.

fields.heading: Documentation and progress reporting
fields.body: For MVA claims, insurers often require treatment plans and progress updates. Our team documents your visits and communicates clearly so you understand next steps in your recovery and claim process.

fields.issue: Lower back pain after long desk hours
fields.approach: We started with a movement screen and found limited hip hinge and weak deep core activation after long sitting. Treatment combined manual therapy for the lower back, progressive core stability drills, and a simple desk break routine every 45 minutes.
fields.outcome: Daily pain dropped from a 7 to a 2 within five weeks. He returned to gym training with a modified program and now manages occasional flare ups with his home exercises. He has not missed work since finishing the plan.

fields.issue: Knee pain during longer runs
fields.approach: A running gait review showed early heel strike and weak left glute medius. We used hip strengthening, cadence cues, and a graded return from walk run intervals to full distance over eight weeks.
fields.outcome: Knee pain during runs resolved by week six. She completed a local 10K without pain and continues a twice weekly strength routine to stay injury free. Her longest run is now back to pre injury distance.

fields.issue: Neck and shoulder tension from screen work
fields.approach: Assessment showed tight upper traps and forward head posture from marking papers and screen time. We used focused neck and shoulder massage, upper back release, and short classroom friendly stretch breaks she could do between classes.
fields.outcome: Headaches went from several per week to rare within a month. She now works full teaching days with much less neck tension. Monthly maintenance sessions help her stay comfortable through the school year.

fields.issue: Stiff mid back when lifting
fields.approach: We found stiff thoracic extension and poor lifting mechanics when loading pallets. Sessions included thoracic joint mobilisation, rib cage mobility work, and coached repetitions of safe lifting patterns with load he uses on the job.
fields.outcome: Morning stiffness that used to last an hour cleared within four weeks. He returned to full warehouse shifts without pain at the end of the day. He still uses the warm up routine before heavy lifting days.

fields.issue: Groin strain during season
fields.approach: Testing showed reduced hip abduction strength and poor single leg control on the injured side. Rehab progressed from band walks and bridges to on ice skating simulation drills and sport specific cutting patterns over twelve weeks.
fields.outcome: He returned to league play at full speed in week ten with no groin recurrence. Strength testing matched his uninjured side before clearance. He continues a twice weekly hip program during the season.

fields.issue: Fear of exercise after knee soreness
fields.approach: She was nervous about exercise after knee soreness on stairs. We built confidence with seated strength work, then progressed to supported squats, balance drills, and a gentle walking plan that increased by five minutes each week.
fields.outcome: Within ten weeks she walks 30 minutes most days without knee pain. She strength trains twice weekly at her community gym with a program we designed together. She reports feeling steadier on stairs and when getting up from chairs.

fields.issue: Persistent shoulder knot from overhead work
fields.approach: We mapped a persistent infraspinatus trigger point referring pain into the deltoid. Dry needling was paired with rotator cuff activation exercises and scapular stability drills performed before and after overhead work shifts.
fields.outcome: Night pain that kept him awake eased after the second session. By week four he could complete a full day of overhead work without needing ice at home. He still does a ten minute shoulder routine before demanding jobs.

fields.issue: Near falls on icy sidewalks
fields.approach: Balance testing showed slow reactive stepping and weak quadriceps on both sides. We used single leg stands, tandem walking, sit to stand power drills, and outdoor practice on uneven paths with a walking pole for confidence.
fields.outcome: Near falls on icy sidewalks stopped after six weeks of consistent practice. She used a cane through winter and walked neighborhood paths independently by spring. She still does her home balance routine three times per week.

fields.issue: Stiff ankle after sprain months ago
fields.approach: Ankle dorsiflexion was limited months after the sprain, affecting his pedal stroke. We combined grade III ankle mobilisations, calf eccentric loading, and a cycling progression from trainer to short outdoor rides as range improved.
fields.outcome: Morning ankle stiffness resolved by week five. He restored a full smooth pedal stroke and completed a 50K charity ride without swelling afterward. He keeps up calf mobility work before longer rides.

fields.issue: Hamstring tightness limiting sprint speed
fields.approach: Video analysis showed reduced hip extension and hamstring tightness during sprinting. We used Nordic hamstring progressions, hip flexor mobility, and sprint drill progressions from submaximal runs to full pace over fourteen weeks.
fields.outcome: His 20 meter sprint time improved by 0.15 seconds and he played a full season without hamstring setbacks. He continues Nordic curls twice weekly in preseason. Coaching staff noted cleaner acceleration form in late season games.

fields.issue: Neck stiffness and headaches after long shifts
fields.approach: Cervical range was limited in rotation and upper traps were constantly tight after long driving shifts. Care included cervical mobilisation, upper back manual release, and a stretching and strengthening plan he could do at rest stops.
fields.outcome: Headache frequency dropped from four per week to one or two per month. Neck rotation improved enough to check blind spots comfortably while driving. He uses his stretch routine before every long haul shift now.

fields.issue: Persistent neck pain despite exercise
fields.approach: She had tried exercise alone with limited relief for persistent neck pain. We added acupuncture twice weekly for four weeks alongside gentle cervical mobility and breathing work to reduce muscle guarding around the upper shoulders.
fields.outcome: Pain scores on a 0 to 10 scale dropped from 6 to 2 over ten weeks. She returned to weekly yoga classes and sleeps through the night without neck waking her. She now uses acupuncture monthly for maintenance during stressful periods.

fields.issue: Chronic hip and IT band tightness
fields.approach: Fascial restrictions along the lateral hip and IT band were limiting comfortable sitting and running. We used sustained myofascial release, glute strengthening, and a gradual return to running from walk run intervals once tissue tolerated load.
fields.outcome: He sits through two hour meetings without needing to stand and stretch constantly. By week nine he completed a 5K run without lateral knee pain for the first time in a year. He foam rolls and does glute activation before runs.

fields.issue: Elbow tendon irritation
fields.approach: Ultrasound was applied before each session to support tendon healing at the elbow. We progressed from isometric wrist holds to slow eccentric lowering exercises with increasing load as grip strength and pain levels allowed.
fields.outcome: Grip pain during serves eased by week four. He returned to league tennis without a brace at week eight and played a full tournament season. He still warms up with eccentric wrist exercises before matches.

fields.issue: Shoulder pain when serving
fields.approach: Scapular dyskinesis was contributing to pain during the serving motion. Kinesio tape supported better shoulder positioning during early rehab while she completed a rotator cuff and scapular stability program three times per week.
fields.outcome: She served a full match with tape support by week three without post match pain. By mid season she competed pain free without tape and maintained her starting position. She still tapes for tournament weekends as a preventive measure.

fields.issue: Sciatica with leg pain when sitting
fields.approach: Repeated extension movements centralised leg pain toward the lower back within two sessions. He performed a specific extension based exercise routine every two hours during workdays plus standing breaks to reduce prolonged flexed sitting.
fields.outcome: Leg pain cleared completely by week three. Sitting tolerance returned to full accounting workdays without needing to lie down after work. He still does his two minute extension routine whenever he feels early back tightness.

fields.issue: Wrist and neck pain with dual monitors
fields.approach: Photo review showed monitors too low and wrists extended during typing. We raised screens to eye level, brought the keyboard closer, and set hourly reminders for ninety second mobility breaks targeting neck, wrists, and upper back.
fields.outcome: Wrist and neck pain that built up by midday dropped noticeably within two weeks. He has not lost a single coding day to pain since making the changes. His employer approved a sit stand desk after our written recommendations.

fields.issue: Room spinning when rolling in bed
fields.approach: Positional testing confirmed benign paroxysmal positional vertigo in the right ear. We performed the Epley maneuver in clinic and taught gaze stabilization exercises to retrain eye head coordination during daily head movements.
fields.outcome: Room spinning when rolling in bed stopped after the second visit. She maintained gains with ten minutes of daily homework and had no recurrence at three month follow up. She feels confident driving and grocery shopping again.

fields.issue: Right hip pain and uneven stride
fields.approach: Assessment showed left hip weakness and a shorter stride on the right. Postural restoration drills focused on left hip grounding, diaphragmatic breathing, and progressive single leg loading before reintroducing running volume.
fields.outcome: Video gait analysis at week eight showed a more even stride length side to side. Right hip pain resolved as he built weekly mileage slowly over eleven weeks. He continues a short breathing and hip drill routine before every run.

fields.issue: Quadriceps weakness after replacement
fields.approach: Quadriceps activation was poor and he could not perform a straight leg raise after surgery. NMES was used before each session to wake up the quads, followed by sit to stand progressions and step ups as strength returned.
fields.outcome: Quad strength testing met surgeon milestones on schedule at nine weeks. He walked without a cane by week six and returned to light hiking by month three. He finished formal physio with a home strength plan he still follows.

fields.issue: Persistent headache and dizziness two weeks after concussion
fields.approach: Assessment showed cervical joint stiffness and exercise intolerance. We combined neck mobilisation, graded aerobic walking, and a return to play protocol aligned with his school and team schedule.
fields.outcome: Headache and dizziness resolved by week three. He completed return to play steps without symptom relapse and returned to full contact practice at week five. His school workload was back to normal with no missed exams.

fields.question: Do I need a doctor referral for physiotherapy or massage in Calgary?
fields.answer: Most extended health plans in Alberta do not require a referral for physiotherapy or massage therapy, but check with your insurer. We provide receipts for reimbursement.

fields.question: How soon after an injury should I book?
fields.answer: Early assessment helps prevent compensations and chronic problems. Book as soon as you can after an acute injury and we will guide you on icing, loading, and next steps.

fields.question: Can I book before my WCB claim is approved?
fields.answer: Yes. Many patients begin with private pay or extended health coverage while a claim is processed. We will explain your options at booking.

fields.question: When should I start physiotherapy after surgery?
fields.answer: Timing depends on your surgery type and surgeon orders. Contact us with your discharge instructions and we will advise on the right start date.

fields.question: Can vestibular therapy help vertigo?
fields.answer: Yes. BPPV is one of the most treatable causes of vertigo. Our physiotherapists perform repositioning maneuvers and teach you how to manage symptoms.

fields.question: When can I start postnatal physiotherapy?
fields.answer: Many patients begin around six weeks postpartum or sooner for specific concerns. We will guide you based on your delivery type and symptoms.

fields.question: Will treatment eliminate my pain completely?
fields.answer: Goals vary by person. Many patients achieve meaningful pain reduction and significant improvement in daily activity. We set honest, measurable goals together.

fields.question: Do I need a referral for pelvic physiotherapy in Alberta?
fields.answer: Referral requirements depend on your insurance plan. Many extended health policies cover pelvic physiotherapy without a doctor note.

fields.question: How long does concussion recovery take?
fields.answer: Most adults recover within two to four weeks, but timelines vary. Early guidance reduces the risk of prolonged symptoms.

fields.question: Does acupuncture hurt?
fields.answer: Needles are very thin. Most people feel a brief tap or dull ache, not sharp pain. Many patients find sessions deeply relaxing.

fields.question: Does physiotherapy hurt?
fields.answer: Some techniques may feel firm, but treatment should stay tolerable. We adjust based on your feedback.

fields.question: How often should I come?
fields.answer: Most patients start weekly, then space visits as symptoms improve.

fields.question: Will I get exercises to do at home?
fields.answer: Yes. Home exercises are a core part of recovery and are tailored to your level.

fields.question: What should I wear?
fields.answer: Comfortable clothing. Most areas are treated while you are draped on the table.

fields.question: Is deep tissue always better?
fields.answer: No. Pressure is matched to your goals and tissue response.

fields.question: Can massage help with injury recovery?
fields.answer: Yes, especially when combined with physiotherapy for structured rehab.

fields.question: Will I hear cracking sounds?
fields.answer: Sometimes joints release with movement. We never force a manipulation.

fields.question: Is manual therapy only for backs?
fields.answer: No. We use it for shoulders, hips, neck, and other joints.

fields.question: How long do results last?
fields.answer: Lasting change usually needs exercise alongside hands on care.

fields.question: Do I need a gym?
fields.answer: No. We start with bands and bodyweight. Gym access helps later phases.

fields.question: Will exercises hurt?
fields.answer: Some muscle effort is normal. Sharp pain means we adjust the plan.

fields.question: Can I keep training?
fields.answer: Often yes, with modified loads while injured tissue heals.

fields.question: How is kinesiology different from physiotherapy?
fields.answer: Kinesiology leans heavily on exercise coaching. Physio may include more hands on care.

fields.question: Do I need equipment?
fields.answer: We start minimal. Bands and simple home items work well.

fields.question: Can kinesiology help before surgery?
fields.answer: Yes. Prehab improves outcomes for many joint procedures.

fields.question: Is dry needling the same as acupuncture?
fields.answer: No. Dry needling targets muscle trigger points. Acupuncture follows traditional meridian theory.

fields.question: Does it hurt?
fields.answer: You may feel a brief twitch or ache. Most patients tolerate it well.

fields.question: Are there side effects?
fields.answer: Mild soreness for a day is common. We review risks before treatment.

fields.question: Am I too old to improve balance?
fields.answer: Most people improve with consistent practice at any age.

fields.question: Do I need special equipment?
fields.answer: We start with chairs and walls. Progress to balance pads when ready.

fields.question: Can this help after a stroke?
fields.answer: Often yes, as part of a broader rehab plan tailored to your needs.

fields.question: Is mobilisation the same as manipulation?
fields.answer: Mobilisation uses smaller graded movements. Manipulation is a quicker thrust technique.

fields.question: Will it fix arthritis?
fields.answer: It cannot reverse arthritis, but it often improves how the joint moves and feels.

fields.question: How soon will I feel change?
fields.answer: Many patients notice easier movement after the first few sessions.

fields.question: Is this only for elite athletes?
fields.answer: No. Recreational runners and gym goers benefit from structured performance work.

fields.question: Will this replace my coach?
fields.answer: We complement coaching with injury screening and corrective work.

fields.question: How often should I train?
fields.answer: Usually 2 to 3 sessions weekly plus your sport practice.

fields.question: Are adjustments safe?
fields.answer: When performed after proper assessment, adjustments are generally safe. We adapt technique to your needs.

fields.question: Will I need ongoing care forever?
fields.answer: Many patients taper to occasional visits once symptoms settle.

fields.question: Do you take X rays in clinic?
fields.answer: We refer for imaging when clinically indicated.

fields.question: Does acupuncture hurt?
fields.answer: Needles are thin. You may feel a brief pinch or dull ache.

fields.question: How many needles are used?
fields.answer: Often 8 to 15 depending on the treatment plan.

fields.question: Can I exercise after?
fields.answer: Light activity is fine. We advise if you should rest the day of treatment.

fields.question: Is this like massage?
fields.answer: Similar hands on work, but focuses on fascia with longer holds.

fields.question: Will I be sore after?
fields.answer: Mild soreness for a day is common. We adjust intensity to your tolerance.

fields.question: How is it different from stretching?
fields.answer: Release works tissue before stretching so range gains last longer.

fields.question: Will I feel heat?
fields.answer: You may feel gentle warmth. Sensation varies by settings.

fields.question: How long is each application?
fields.answer: Usually 5 to 8 minutes per area.

fields.question: Is ultrasound enough on its own?
fields.answer: No. Exercise and load management drive lasting recovery.

fields.question: How long does tape stay on?
fields.answer: Usually 3 to 5 days if skin tolerates it.

fields.question: Can I shower with it?
fields.answer: Yes. Pat dry afterward.

fields.question: Does tape replace bracing?
fields.answer: It is lighter than rigid braces. We choose based on injury needs.

fields.question: Is McKenzie only for backs?
fields.answer: It is used for neck, back, and some extremity issues.

fields.question: What if movements hurt?
fields.answer: We find the direction that helps. Wrong direction is stopped immediately.

fields.question: Will I need to exercise forever?

fields.content:
If you were hurt at work in Calgary, physiotherapy is often one of the first treatments WCB Alberta approves. At Medpro Physiotherapy, we regularly see patients from Falconridge, Martindale, and across northeast Calgary who need help recovering from strains, sprains, back pain, and repetitive strain injuries.

The process can feel confusing when you are already dealing with pain. This guide explains what WCB covers, what happens at your first appointment, and how to set yourself up for a smoother recovery.

What is WCB Alberta and when does it apply?

WCB Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board) provides benefits when you are injured at work or develop an occupational illness. If your claim is accepted, WCB may cover approved medical treatment, including physiotherapy, massage therapy, and related rehabilitation services.

Most Alberta employers are required to carry WCB coverage. After an injury, you should report the incident to your supervisor and seek medical attention if needed. Your doctor or nurse practitioner may recommend physiotherapy as part of your recovery plan.

How physiotherapy helps workplace injuries

Workplace injuries often involve the back, neck, shoulders, knees, or wrists. Physiotherapy addresses pain, stiffness, weakness, and poor movement patterns that develop after an injury or during modified duties.

  • Hands on treatment to reduce pain and improve joint mobility
  • Targeted exercises to rebuild strength and endurance
  • Education on posture, lifting technique, and pacing at work
  • Gradual return to work planning with your employer when appropriate
  • Progress notes for WCB so your claim stays on track

What to bring to your first WCB physiotherapy visit

Having the right information at your first appointment saves time and helps us start treatment sooner. Please bring the following to our Falconridge Blvd clinic:

  • Your WCB claim number (if you have one)
  • Alberta health card and photo ID
  • Details about how the injury happened and your job duties
  • Any medical reports, X rays, or MRI results
  • A list of medications and previous treatments
  • Work restrictions or modified duty notes from your employer or doctor

What happens during your assessment

Your first visit usually takes 45 to 60 minutes. Your physiotherapist will ask about your injury history, work tasks, pain levels, and goals. We then assess movement, strength, and function in the affected area.

From there, we create a treatment plan tailored to your injury and job demands. Many patients notice some relief within the first few sessions, although full recovery depends on the type and severity of the injury.

Our goal is not just to reduce pain. We want you to move confidently and return to work when it is safe, with strategies to prevent re injury.

Common questions about WCB and physiotherapy

Every claim is different, but most patients want to know how long treatment will last, whether they need a referral, and how scheduling works around work shifts. We coordinate with WCB requirements and keep communication clear throughout your care.

If you are unsure whether your injury qualifies, contact WCB Alberta or speak with your employer's safety or HR team. You can also call our clinic and we will guide you on what information to gather before booking.

fields.content:
Massage therapy is one of the most requested services at our northeast Calgary clinic. Patients come to us with tight shoulders from desk work, sore backs after weekend activities, headaches linked to neck tension, and muscle fatigue from training or physically demanding jobs.

Unlike a spa style relaxation massage, therapeutic massage at a physiotherapy and wellness clinic focuses on specific areas of tension, movement restrictions, and recovery goals. Here is how it works and when it may be right for you.

What therapeutic massage treats

Registered massage therapists use hands on techniques to influence muscles, connective tissue, and circulation. Treatment can help with both recent injuries and longer standing discomfort.

  • Neck and shoulder tension from computer work or driving
  • Lower back stiffness and muscle spasms
  • Sports related muscle soreness and overuse
  • Headaches associated with neck and upper back tension
  • Stress related muscle tightness
  • Recovery support after physiotherapy or surgery (when cleared by your care team)

Massage therapy vs relaxation massage

Both can feel calming, but therapeutic massage is structured around assessment and outcomes. Your therapist will ask about your pain patterns, activities, and health history before treatment begins.

Pressure is adjusted throughout the session. Some areas may need deeper work while others require a lighter approach. Communication is important. Speak up if anything feels uncomfortable.

Many of our Calgary patients combine massage with physiotherapy or chiropractic care for better overall results, especially when pain involves both joints and surrounding muscles.

When to book massage therapy in Calgary

You do not need to wait until pain is severe. Massage can be helpful at different stages of recovery and prevention.

  • When muscle tension is limiting your sleep, work, or exercise
  • After a physiotherapy assessment identifies soft tissue restrictions
  • During a busy season at work when stress and posture are taking a toll
  • As part of a maintenance plan for active lifestyles or manual labour jobs
  • When your extended health plan includes massage therapy coverage

What to expect at your appointment

Your first visit includes a brief health history and discussion of your goals. Treatment may involve Swedish techniques, deep tissue work, trigger point release, or stretching depending on your needs.

Sessions typically last 30, 45, or 60 minutes. Mild soreness for a day or two can happen after deeper work, similar to post exercise stiffness. Drinking water and gentle movement often help.

If you have a new injury, unexplained swelling, fever, or a condition that requires medical clearance, tell your therapist before treatment. Safety always comes first.

Insurance and booking in Calgary

Many Alberta extended health plans cover registered massage therapy. We provide receipts for reimbursement and can direct bill select insurers. Check your policy for annual limits and whether a prescription is required.

Our clinic is located at 1130-367 Nolanridge Cr NW in Calgary, with convenient access for patients across northwest Calgary. You can book online or call to find a time that fits your schedule.

fields.author: Medpro Physiotherapy Team
fields.content:
Starting physiotherapy is a positive step toward feeling better. Whether you were referred by your doctor, booked after a sports injury, or finally decided to address that nagging shoulder pain, knowing what to expect can make your first visit much easier.

At Medpro Physiotherapy in northeast Calgary, we see many first time patients each month. Here is a straightforward guide to help you prepare.

Before you arrive

A little preparation goes a long way. Aim to arrive five to ten minutes early so you can complete any remaining intake details at reception.

  • Alberta health card and photo ID
  • Extended health insurance information (if applicable)
  • WCB claim number or MVA insurance details (if your visit is related to a claim)
  • Referral letter or imaging reports (X ray, ultrasound, MRI)
  • List of current medications and relevant medical history
  • Comfortable clothing, such as shorts for a knee issue or a tank top for shoulder treatment

Your assessment: what we ask and what we look at

Your physiotherapist will start by understanding your story. Expect questions about when symptoms began, what makes them better or worse, your work and hobbies, and what you hope to achieve through treatment.

We then perform a physical assessment. This may include checking posture, joint movement, muscle strength, balance, and functional tasks like squatting, reaching, or walking. The goal is to identify what is driving your symptoms, not just where you feel pain.

Good physiotherapy looks at the whole picture. Your knee pain might relate to hip strength, foot mechanics, or how you move at work. We connect those dots before recommending treatment.

Treatment on day one

Many first visits include some hands on treatment or guided exercises if appropriate. This might involve manual therapy, soft tissue work, acupuncture, taping, or education on posture and pacing.

You will also receive home exercises tailored to your condition. Consistency between visits often makes the biggest difference in how quickly you improve.

Your personalized treatment plan

Before you leave, we explain our findings and outline a plan. This includes recommended visit frequency, expected timeline for improvement, and milestones to track progress.

Plans are adjusted as you improve. Some conditions need only a few sessions. Others, such as post surgical rehab or chronic pain, may require longer term care with periodic reviews.

  • Short term goals: reduce pain, improve daily movement
  • Medium term goals: return to exercise, work, or sport
  • Long term goals: build resilience and prevent recurrence

Tips for getting the most from physiotherapy

Be honest about your symptoms and activity levels. If exercises are too hard or too easy, say so. If something hurts during treatment, let your therapist know right away.

Keep up with home exercises and follow activity modifications we suggest. Small daily habits often matter more than occasional clinic visits alone.

Our Calgary clinic offers physiotherapy, massage therapy, chiropractic care, acupuncture, and kinesiology under one roof. If your plan would benefit from another service, we can coordinate your care internally.

fields.content:
After joint replacement, ligament repair, or other orthopedic surgery, your body needs a clear plan to heal well. At Medpro Physiotherapy in northwest Calgary, we help patients recover from knee and hip replacements, rotator cuff repairs, ACL reconstruction, and other procedures with step by step rehab.

The right timing and exercises matter. Too much too soon can irritate healing tissue; too little can lead to stiffness and weakness. Physiotherapy bridges that gap.

Early phase: protection and mobility

The first weeks often emphasize reducing swelling, managing pain within safe limits, and restoring basic movement. Your therapist will review surgical protocols from your surgeon and tailor treatment to your date of surgery and current restrictions.

  • Gentle range of motion exercises within approved limits
  • Swelling and scar management strategies
  • Safe walking, stairs, and transfers with assistive devices if needed
  • Breathing and circulation exercises after certain surgeries

Building strength and function

As healing progresses, rehab shifts toward strength, balance, and tasks that matter to you, returning to work, driving, hiking, or sport. We set milestones so you know what normal soreness looks like versus a warning sign to slow down.

Good post surgical rehab is not about rushing. It is about steady progress with exercises you can repeat confidently at home.

Working with your care team

We communicate using your surgeon's guidelines and document progress at each visit. If something feels off, sudden swelling, sharp pain, or loss of function, we adjust the plan and recommend medical follow up when appropriate.

Many patients combine physiotherapy with massage therapy for muscle tension around the surgical area once cleared by their care team.

Early physiotherapy focuses on swelling control, range of motion, and walking confidence.
Progressive strengthening and functional training come next, not on day one.

fields.title: The Role of Physiotherapy in Managing Chronic Pain in Calgary
fields.meta_title: Chronic Pain Physiotherapy Calgary | Medpro Physiotherapy
fields.meta_description: Understand how physiotherapy helps chronic pain in Calgary through movement, education, and hands on care. Practical strategies from Medpro Physiotherapy.
fields.summary: Chronic pain is complex, but movement, pacing, and targeted treatment can improve how you feel and function day to day.
fields.image_alt: Physiotherapist discussing chronic pain management with a patient
fields.author: Medpro Physiotherapy Team
fields.content:
Pain that lasts months or years can affect work, sleep, mood, and confidence. Patients at our Nolanridge Court clinic often describe back pain, neck tension, headaches, or widespread soreness that flares with activity or stress.

Physiotherapy for chronic pain does not promise instant relief. It focuses on helping you understand your pain, rebuild tolerance for movement, and regain control over daily routines.

Why movement helps, carefully

Avoiding all activity can increase stiffness and fear of movement. The goal is a gradual return to walking, stretching, and strengthening at a level your nervous system can handle.

  • Mobility work for stiff joints and tight muscles
  • Strength training for postural and core support
  • Aerobic activity such as walking or cycling, progressed slowly
  • Relaxation and breathing techniques for flare ups

Hands on care and other tools

Manual therapy, massage, acupuncture, and dry needling may reduce muscle tension that contributes to pain. These work best alongside an active plan, not instead of one.

Flare ups happen. Physiotherapy teaches you how to respond, adjust activity, use strategies you have practiced, and get back on track without feeling like you have lost all progress.

Setting realistic goals

Success might mean sleeping better, walking 20 minutes comfortably, or returning to a hobby, not necessarily zero pain. We track function and quality of life, not just a pain number on a scale.

Gradual, consistent movement is usually safer and more effective than complete rest.
Pacing, sleep, and stress management are part of recovery, not extras.

paragraphs: Manual therapy, massage, acupuncture, and dry needling may reduce muscle tension that contributes to pain. These work best alongside an active plan, not instead of one.
sections.blockquote: Flare ups happen. Physiotherapy teaches you how to respond, adjust activity, use strategies you have practiced, and get back on track without feeling like you have lost all progress.

sections.heading: Setting realistic goals
paragraphs: Success might mean sleeping better, walking 20 minutes comfortably, or returning to a hobby, not necessarily zero pain. We track function and quality of life, not just a pain number on a scale.

faqs: Is chronic pain all in my head?
Pain is always real. Stress and mood can amplify it, but tissue sensitivity, posture, and activity patterns also play a role. Treatment addresses the whole picture.
How long does chronic pain physiotherapy take?
Timelines vary widely. Some patients improve over weeks; others benefit from longer maintenance plans with periodic check ins.
Can massage or chiropractic care help chronic pain too?
Yes, many patients combine services. We can coordinate care within our clinic when multiple approaches fit your plan.

fields.meta_description: Not sure if you need physio? Learn five common signs, from lingering pain to balance issues, and when to book at Medpro Physiotherapy in northwest Calgary.
fields.summary: Pain that sticks around, limits your sport, or wakes you at night is worth a professional assessment. Here are five clear signs to book physiotherapy.
fields.image_alt: Patient consulting a physiotherapist about pain symptoms
fields.author: Medpro Physiotherapy Team
fields.content:
Many people postpone physiotherapy, hoping pain will pass on its own. Sometimes it does. When symptoms persist or interfere with work, sleep, or exercise, an assessment can prevent a small issue from becoming a long term problem.

1. Pain that lasts longer than expected

Most soft tissue injuries improve within days to a few weeks with basic rest and movement. If pain continues beyond that window, or keeps returning in the same area, physiotherapy can identify contributing factors such as weakness, stiff joints, or poor movement habits.

2. Pain that limits daily activities or sport

Trouble lifting groceries, sitting at your desk, running, or playing with your kids are practical reasons to seek help. Treatment targets the movements that matter to you.

3. Numbness, tingling, or weakness

These symptoms can relate to nerve irritation in the neck, back, or limbs. Physiotherapists assess whether conservative care is appropriate or if medical imaging or referral is needed.

4. Balance, dizziness, or falls

Vestibular and balance issues respond well to specialized physiotherapy. Do not dismiss near falls or room spinning episodes, especially if they are new or worsening.

5. You are relying on pain medication alone

Medication can help short term, but it rarely fixes the underlying movement problem. Combining physiotherapy with medical care often leads to better long term outcomes.

You can book online at our northwest Calgary clinic or call if you are unsure which service fits, physiotherapy, massage, or chiropractic, and we will point you in the right direction.
key_takeaways: Pain lasting more than a few weeks without improvement deserves an assessment.
Reduced range of motion or strength often shows up before serious injury.
Balance problems, dizziness, or repeated falls should be checked promptly.
You do not need to wait until pain is severe, early care often means faster recovery.

fields.title: Dry Needling in Calgary: How It Works and Who Can Benefit
fields.meta_title: Dry Needling Calgary | Benefits & What to Expect
fields.meta_description: Dry needling in Calgary can ease muscle trigger points and tension. Learn how it differs from acupuncture and who may benefit at Medpro Physiotherapy.
fields.summary: Dry needling uses thin needles to release tight muscle bands and improve movement. Here is how it works, who it helps, and what to expect at your visit.
fields.image_alt: Physiotherapist performing dry needling treatment in Calgary
fields.author: Medpro Physiotherapy Team
fields.content:
Dry needling is a technique used by trained physiotherapists and other regulated clinicians to treat myofascial trigger points, tight bands in muscle that can refer pain elsewhere. At Medpro Physiotherapy, it is one tool we may use alongside manual therapy and exercise.

Although the needles look similar to acupuncture, the reasoning and placement are different. Dry needling is based on musculoskeletal assessment; traditional acupuncture follows Eastern medicine principles. Some patients receive both types of care for different goals.

What happens during a dry needling session

After assessing your movement and pain patterns, your therapist inserts a thin, sterile needle into a targeted muscle. You may feel a quick cramp or twitch response. Needles stay in briefly or are moved gently depending on the technique used.

  • Sessions are often 15 to 30 minutes within a longer physiotherapy visit
  • Mild soreness for a day afterward is common, similar to deep massage
  • Hydration and light movement usually help post treatment comfort

Who may benefit

Dry needling can help athletes, desk workers, and post injury patients with persistent muscle tension that has not responded fully to stretching alone. It is not appropriate for everyone, your therapist will screen for medical conditions, pregnancy, and needle sensitivity.

Needling alone rarely solves the whole problem. We pair it with strengthening and movement retraining so results last.
key_takeaways: Dry needling targets tight muscle trigger points, not acupuncture meridians.
It is often used for neck, shoulder, back, and hip muscle tension.
Most patients feel a brief twitch or ache during treatment, then relief or improved movement.
It works best as part of a plan that includes exercise and education.

faqs: Does dry needling hurt?
You may feel a brief ache or twitch when the needle contacts a trigger point. Most people tolerate it well and report less muscle tightness afterward.
Is dry needling the same as acupuncture?
No. Acupuncture follows traditional Chinese medicine points and theory. Dry needling focuses on Western anatomy and trigger points in muscle.
How many sessions will I need?
Some patients notice improvement after one or two sessions; others need several visits combined with exercise. Your therapist will recommend a plan after your assessment.
